meta.tagline: Curriculum-aligned teaching resources for Ghanaian basic schools
meta.curriculum: NaCCA Standards-Based Curriculum (2019) for Basic 1-6 · Common Core Programme for JHS 1-3

officialDocs.note: Official curriculum documents published free by NaCCA (nacca.gov.gh). We link to them so you always have the authoritative source — we do not rehost or alter them.

resources.title: Counting, Grouping and Place Value to 100
resources.subject: Mathematics
resources.contentStandard: Demonstrate understanding of numbers up to 100 in terms of counting, grouping, and place value.
resources.indicator: Count, group, and represent numbers up to 100 using concrete objects, drawings, and numerals.
outcomes: Learner counts objects up to 100 in tens and ones.
Learner represents a number on a place-value chart.
steps: Warm-up (5 min): Skip counting in 2s and 5s using a rhyme or clapping game.
Pair activity (15 min): Learners get bundles of bottle tops/sticks to count and bundle into tens.
Representation (10 min): Learners show their count as tens and ones on a place-value chart.
Individual practice (10 min): Worksheet matching numeral, word, and grouped objects.
Wrap-up (5 min): 3 learners share their groupings with the class.
resources.assessment: Learner correctly groups and states the number of objects (tens and ones) for 3 out of 4 sets.
resources.notes: Use locally available counters. Learners who finish early can bundle 3 numbers into tens and compare.

resources.title: The Water Cycle and Why It Matters
resources.subject: Science
resources.contentStandard: Understand the water cycle and its importance to living things.
resources.indicator: Explain the processes involved in the water cycle (evaporation, condensation, precipitation, collection).
outcomes: Learner names and explains the 4 stages of the water cycle.
Learner relates the water cycle to farming and drinking water in the community.
steps: Recap (5 min): Ask learners where rain comes from — collect their existing ideas.
Demonstration (15 min): Boil water in a covered pot in class (or show a diagram/video) to observe evaporation and condensation.
Group activity (15 min): Learners sequence picture cards of the 4 water cycle stages and label them.
Discussion (10 min): Why the water cycle matters for farming and drinking water in their community.
Exit ticket (10 min): Learners draw and label a simple water cycle diagram.
materials: Pot and heat source (or diagram/video alternative)
resources.assessment: Learner correctly sequences and labels all 4 stages of the water cycle.
resources.notes: Safety first with the heat source. A diagram or video works when a live demonstration is not possible.

resources.title: Local Government: The Role of the District Assembly
resources.subject: Social Studies
resources.contentStandard: Demonstrate understanding of the structure and functions of local government in Ghana.
resources.indicator: Explain the roles of the District/Municipal/Metropolitan Assembly in local governance.
outcomes: Learner explains at least 3 functions of a District Assembly.
Learner identifies the key officers of an Assembly.
steps: Starter (5 min): Learners name a recent local project (road, market, school) and who they think provided it.
Direct teaching (15 min): Structure of Assemblies — Assembly member, MCE/DCE, sub-committees.
Case study (10 min): A short real example of an Assembly project in a Ghanaian district.
Group task (15 min): Role-play a mini Assembly meeting debating a local issue (e.g., waste management).
Reflection (5 min): One thing learners would raise if they were Assembly members.
resources.assessment: Learner explains at least 3 functions of a District Assembly in their own words.
resources.notes: Choose a case study from your own district whenever possible — it makes the lesson instantly relevant.

resources.title: Building Good Sentences: Naming and Doing Words
resources.subject: English Language
resources.contentStandard: Recognise and use naming words (nouns) and doing words (verbs) to form simple sentences.
resources.indicator: Identify nouns and verbs in sentences and construct simple sentences of 3-6 words correctly.
outcomes: Learner identifies nouns and verbs in a given sentence.
Learner builds a correct simple sentence using a naming word and a doing word.
steps: Warm-up (5 min): Action game — teacher says a word, learners act it out if it is a 'doing word'.
Direct teaching (10 min): Sorting flashcards into two hoops on the board: THINGS/PEOPLE/PLACES (naming words) vs ACTIONS (doing words).

Guided practice (10 min): Build sentences on the board from two cards, e.g. 'The dog' + 'is barking' = a full sentence. Check: does it make sense? Does it start with a capital and end with a full stop?
Pair work (10 min): Each pair draws one noun card and one verb card and builds a sentence, then reads it aloud.
Independent work (10 min): Worksheet — underline naming words, circle doing words, write 2 sentences of their own.
resources.assessment: Learner sorts at least 8 of 10 word cards correctly and writes one complete sentence with correct capital letter and full stop.
resources.notes: Use pictures from Ghanaian daily life (market, trotro, kente) so every learner recognises the nouns instantly.

resources.title: Reading Comprehension: Finding Answers in a Story
resources.subject: English Language
resources.contentStandard: Read simple texts fluently and demonstrate understanding by answering literal questions.
resources.indicator: Answer who, what, where and when questions from a short passage.
outcomes: Learner reads a short passage aloud with growing fluency.
Learner answers at least 4 of 6 literal comprehension questions correctly.
steps: Pre-reading (5 min): Show the story title and picture; learners predict what will happen.
First reading (10 min): Teacher reads aloud while learners follow with a finger; discuss new words on the word wall.
Second reading (10 min): Learners read aloud in pairs, taking turns by paragraph.
Question work (10 min): Model finding an answer by 'hunting' in the text — underline the sentence that answers the question.
Independent practice (10 min): Six written questions (who, what, where, when) answered in full sentences.
resources.assessment: Learner answers at least 4 of 6 literal questions correctly, with at least 2 answered in full sentences.
resources.notes: Choose stories with Ghanaian settings and names — comprehension improves dramatically when the context is familiar.

resources.title: Punctuation That Changes Meaning
resources.subject: English Language
resources.contentStandard: Use punctuation marks correctly to make writing clear and meaningful.
resources.indicator: Use full stops, question marks, exclamation marks, commas and apostrophes correctly in own writing.
outcomes: Learner explains how punctuation changes meaning.
Learner punctuates an unpunctuated paragraph with at least 80% accuracy.
steps: Hook (5 min): Write two sentences on the board — 'Let us eat, Grandma' vs 'Let us eat Grandma' — and let learners discover the difference.
Direct teaching (10 min): Full stop, question mark, exclamation mark, comma (lists and pauses), apostrophe (contractions and possession) with board examples.
Guided practice (10 min): Class punctuates 5 sentences together, justifying each choice.
Pair work (15 min): Pairs punctuate a short unpunctuated paragraph, then swap with another pair to mark.
Application (10 min): Learners write 3 sentences about their morning, using at least one comma and one apostrophe correctly.
resources.assessment: Learner punctuates the paragraph correctly in at least 8 of 10 marked spots.
resources.notes: Keep a permanent punctuation wall chart; refer to it during every composition lesson.

resources.title: Writing a Composition: My Community
resources.subject: English Language
resources.contentStandard: Write a well-organised descriptive composition with a clear beginning, middle and end.
resources.indicator: Plan, draft and write a 3-paragraph composition using descriptive language and correct punctuation.
outcomes: Learner plans a composition using a mind-map.
Learner writes 3 connected paragraphs with an introduction, description and conclusion.
steps: Model (10 min): Teacher displays a short model paragraph 'My Community' and labels its parts: topic sentence, supporting details, closing sentence.
Brainstorm (10 min): Class mind-map on the board — places, people, sounds, smells, problems and prides of the community.
Planning (10 min): Each learner picks 3 favourite ideas from the mind-map onto a planning sheet.
Drafting (20 min): Learners write 3 paragraphs; teacher moves round prompting with questions (What can you see? Who lives near you? What would you change?).
Peer review (10 min): Partners read each other's work and give one star (praise) and one wish (suggestion).
resources.assessment: Learner's composition has 3 paragraphs, at least 3 concrete details from the mind-map, and correct sentence ends.
resources.notes: Display the best compositions on the class wall — learners write better for an audience.

resources.title: Formal Letter Writing
resources.subject: English Language
resources.contentStandard: Write formal letters for real-life purposes using the correct layout, register and conventions.
resources.indicator: Write a formal letter with correct address placement, salutation, body structure and subscription.
outcomes: Learner identifies the 5 parts of a formal letter in the correct order.
Learner writes a formal letter applying for something real (e.g., school requests).
steps: Analyse (10 min): Project or draw a model formal letter; learners label the 5 parts — sender's address, date, receiver's address, salutation, body, subscription.
Register talk (10 min): Compare informal vs formal language — 'Chale, please' vs 'I respectfully request'. Collect formal phrases: 'I am writing to…', 'I would be grateful…', 'Yours faithfully'.
Guided layout (10 min): Class dictates a letter to the head teacher requesting a reading club; teacher writes the skeleton on the board.
Independent writing (25 min): Learners write their own letter (choose from: requesting a school library book, requesting a PTA meeting, applying to join a school club).
Checking (5 min): Checklist swap — partner checks layout order and salutation-subscription match (Dear Sir/Madam → Yours faithfully).
resources.assessment: Learner's letter contains all 5 parts in correct order and maintains formal register throughout.
resources.notes: Formal letters are tested in BECE and used in real life — link to an actual school need so learners write for a purpose.

resources.title: Fractions: Halves, Quarters and Equivalents
resources.subject: Mathematics
resources.contentStandard: Demonstrate understanding of fractions as parts of a whole and compare simple fractions.
resources.indicator: Find halves and quarters of shapes and quantities; identify simple equivalent fractions.
outcomes: Learner finds a half and a quarter of a shape and of a quantity.
Learner identifies at least 2 equivalent fractions using paper folding.
steps: Warm-up (5 min): Quick mental maths — find half of 10, 20, 50, 100.
Folding activity (15 min): Learners fold paper strips to show halves, quarters, eighths; shade and label each fold.
Discovery (10 min): Hold up folded strips — which shaded parts match? Establish equivalence (2/4 = 1/2, 4/8 = 1/2) visually.
Quantity work (10 min): Use bottle tops — find 1/2 and 1/4 of 12, 16, 20 bottle tops.
Practice (10 min): Worksheet — shade fractions of shapes and find fractions of numbers.
resources.assessment: Learner correctly finds fractions of 3 out of 4 quantities and shows one equivalent pair.
resources.notes: Connect to real life: sharing kenkey, dividing a football pitch, sharing transport fares.

resources.title: Operations on Integers
resources.subject: Mathematics
resources.contentStandard: Perform operations on integers and apply them to real-life contexts.
resources.indicator: Add, subtract, multiply and divide integers using the number line and rules of signs.
outcomes: Learner adds and subtracts directed numbers using a number line.
Learner applies the rules of signs when multiplying and dividing integers.
steps: Context hook (5 min): Temperature at dawn (-5°C) rising to 12°C — how much did it change? Money owed vs money in hand.
Number line (15 min): Learners move counters on a large floor/board number line for (-3) + 8, 5 - 9, (-2) - (-6).
Rules of signs (10 min): Derive and record — same signs multiply to positive, different signs to negative. Class chant the rules.
Practice ladder (15 min): Mixed exercise from easy (4 - 7) to harder ((-6) × (-5)), learners self-check with a partner.
Real-life challenge (10 min): Write an integer story for a classmate, e.g., 'Kwame borrows GHC5, then repays GHC8' — model it with integers.
resources.assessment: Learner solves at least 8 of 10 mixed integer operations correctly.
resources.notes: Insist on reasoning language: 'minus three plus eight means starting at -3 and moving 8 steps right'.

resources.title: Living and Non-Living Things
resources.subject: Science
resources.contentStandard: Distinguish between living and non-living things based on their characteristics.
resources.indicator: Identify and sort living and non-living things using the characteristics of life.
outcomes: Learner states 3 characteristics of living things.
Learner sorts 10 items into living and non-living correctly (at least 8/10).
steps: Hook (5 min): Bring out a stone and a potted seedling — 'Which one is alive? How do you know?'
Direct teaching (10 min): Characteristics of living things — they grow, breathe/respire, feed, move by themselves, reproduce, respond. Learners echo-check with each example.
Sorting game (15 min): Stations with picture cards and real items (stone, leaf, feather, pin, water, plant, insect picture) — teams sort and justify.
Walk and spot (10 min): Quick observation walk around the school compound listing 3 living and 3 non-living things.
Consolidation (5 min): Exit question — 'Is fire alive? Is a stone alive?' with reasoning.
resources.assessment: Learner sorts 8 of 10 items correctly and gives one reason using a characteristic of living things.
resources.notes: Handle the tricky cases: fire, cars, clouds — use the 'does it do it by itself?' test.

resources.title: Elements, Compounds and Mixtures
resources.subject: Science
resources.contentStandard: Classify matter as elements, compounds or mixtures based on their composition.
resources.indicator: Distinguish between elements, compounds and mixtures using examples and simple demonstrations.
outcomes: Learner defines element, compound and mixture with one example each.
Learner classifies 8 substances correctly.
steps: Recap (5 min): What is matter? Everything made of particles.

Direct teaching (15 min): Element = one kind of particle only (iron, copper, oxygen); Compound = two or more elements chemically joined (water, salt, sugar); Mixture = substances physically mixed (air, salad, sand and salt). Use simple particle diagrams on the board.
Demo (10 min): Mix iron filings and sulphur powder in a dish — still a mixture (can separate with a magnet). Compare with a compound that cannot be separated this way.
Sorting activity (15 min): Groups classify substance cards (gold, water, air, salt, rust, brass, oxygen, chalk) into E/C/M columns.
Application (10 min): Each group presents one tricky classification with a reason.
resources.assessment: Learner classifies at least 6 of 8 substances correctly with a reason for two of them.
resources.notes: Relate to local materials: gold (element), shea butter mixture, salt from lagoon water (compound dissolved in mixture).

resources.title: Water in My Community: Sources and Uses
resources.subject: Our World Our People
resources.contentStandard: Identify sources of water and demonstrate responsible use of water in daily life.
resources.indicator: Name at least 3 sources of water and 5 uses of water at home and in school.
outcomes: Learner names 3 sources of water in the community.
Learner lists 5 uses of water and one way to save water.
steps: Picture starter (5 min): Show pictures — borehole, river, polytank, tap, sachet water. Where does our water come from?
Sharing (10 min): Learners describe how their household gets and stores water; teacher lists sources on chart.
Uses brainstorm (10 min): Picture-sort of uses — drinking, cooking, bathing, washing, watering plants, feeding animals.
Saving water talk (10 min): Why water is precious — simple saving habits (close the tap, reuse, don't play with drinking water).
Activity (10 min): Learners draw their main water source and label 3 uses.
resources.assessment: Learner names 3 sources, 5 uses and 1 water-saving habit.
resources.notes: Link to hygiene lessons — safe water and handwashing go together.

resources.title: Sources of History: How We Know About the Past
resources.subject: History of Ghana
resources.contentStandard: Understand what history is and identify the main sources of historical information.
resources.indicator: Classify sources of history as primary or secondary and evaluate their usefulness.
outcomes: Learner defines history as the study of past events.
Learner sorts 6 sources into primary and secondary with reasons.
steps: Mystery starter (5 min): Show an old family photo, a folk song and a written diary page — how would someone in 100 years know about us?
Direct teaching (15 min): Primary sources (created at the time: artefacts, buildings, photographs, diaries, songs, oral traditions) vs secondary sources (written later: textbooks, articles).
Sorting game (15 min): Teams race to sort source cards and justify placements.
Local detective work (10 min): Learners name one primary source in their own community (a chief's stool, an old shrine, a monument, an elder's memory).
Reflection (5 min): Why do historians need more than one source? (Evidence must agree.)
resources.assessment: Learner sorts 5 of 6 sources correctly and states one reason why oral tradition is both useful and needing care.
resources.notes: Invite an elder for the next lesson — a live primary source makes this unforgettable.

resources.title: Honesty: Telling the Truth in Daily Life
resources.subject: Religious & Moral Education
resources.strand: Religious Practices and their Moral Implications
resources.contentStandard: Demonstrate honesty and truthfulness in relationships at home, school and community.
resources.indicator: Explain why honesty is important and demonstrate honest behaviour in given scenarios.
outcomes: Learner explains in own words why telling the truth matters.
Learner suggests honest responses in at least 2 of 3 scenarios.
steps: Story starter (10 min): Tell a short story of a child who broke something and told the truth — what happened next?
Discussion (10 min): What is a lie? What happens to trust when we lie? (Broken trust, blame, punishment, shame).

Scenario cards (15 min): Small groups decide what an honest response looks like — 'You accidentally broke your friend's pencil…', 'You didn't do your homework…', 'The trader gave you too much change…'.
Commitment (5 min): Each learner writes/Draws one honest promise for the week.
Song/closure (5 min): Simple honesty song or class motto.
resources.assessment: Learner gives honest responses to 2 of 3 scenarios and explains one benefit of honesty.
resources.notes: Praise honest confessions immediately — it teaches that truth-telling is safe here.

resources.title: Parts of a Computer and Their Uses
resources.subject: Computing
resources.contentStandard: Identify the main parts of a computer system and describe their functions.
resources.indicator: Identify input, output, processing and storage devices and state their uses.
outcomes: Learner names 5 parts of a computer and their functions.
Learner classifies devices as input or output.
steps: Hook (5 min): Without a computer in the room? No problem — use pictures, or a laptop brought from home, or a phone comparison.

Direct teaching (15 min): The computer family — Input (keyboard, mouse, microphone: putting information IN), Output (monitor, printer, speakers: information OUT), Processing (CPU: the brain), Storage (hard drive, pendrive, memory card).
Classification game (15 min): Device cards sorted into INPUT / OUTPUT / BOTH boards.
Real connect (10 min): Learners find input/output examples on a phone (touchscreen = input AND output — surprise!).
Quick quiz (5 min): 5 rapid-fire questions.
resources.assessment: Learner classifies 8 of 10 devices correctly and states the function of any 3.
resources.notes: No lab required — this lesson works fully with printed cards and drawings.

resources.title: Components of a Computer System
resources.subject: Computing
resources.contentStandard: Describe the components of a computer system and how they work together.
resources.indicator: Differentiate between hardware and software and describe the functions of system units.
outcomes: Learner distinguishes hardware from software with 2 examples each.
Learner traces the input → processing → output → storage flow.
steps: Review (5 min): Input/output devices from primary school — now deeper.

Direct teaching (15 min): Hardware (physical parts: system unit, peripherals) vs Software (programs: system software vs application software). The four-step flow: input → processing → output, with storage alongside.
Analogy work (10 min): Body analogy — hardware = body, system software = the brain's instincts, application software = skills. Learners map other analogies.
Diagram task (15 min): Learners draw and label a computer system flow diagram for their own scenario (e.g., typing an essay: keyboard → CPU → monitor → save to pendrive).
Quick assessment (5 min): 5 questions on hardware/software classification.
resources.assessment: Learner's diagram correctly shows the flow with at least 2 hardware and 2 software examples.
resources.notes: Collect junk hardware (old keyboard, mouse, cables) for a permanent display table.

resources.title: Locomotor Movements: Walk, Run, Jump and Hop
resources.subject: Physical Education
resources.contentStandard: Perform basic locomotor movements with control and in response to signals.
resources.indicator: Demonstrate walking, running, jumping and hopping with correct form.
outcomes: Learner performs 4 locomotor movements with control.
Learner responds correctly to movement signals.
steps: Warm-up (5 min): Stretch and shake every body part to a counting rhyme.
Teach and practise (15 min): Each movement shown and practised — walking tall, running with bent arms, jumping from two feet, hopping on one foot. Mark out lanes with stones/pebbles.
Movement game (10 min): 'Red light, green light' variations — teacher calls a movement, learners perform it moving across the field.
Relay (5 min): Two teams race using one assigned movement per round.
Cool down (5 min): Breathing and stretch; count heartbeats before and after to feel exercise working.
resources.assessment: Learner demonstrates all 4 movements with control when called randomly.
resources.notes: No equipment needed. Always check the field for glass/sharp objects before class.

resources.title: Creating Patterns from Nature
resources.subject: Creative Arts
resources.contentStandard: Use elements of art (line, shape, colour, texture) to create patterns inspired by nature and the environment.
resources.indicator: Design and produce a pattern based on natural objects, using repeated motifs.
outcomes: Learner identifies pattern in natural objects and Ghanaian textiles.
Learner creates a repeating pattern using at least 2 natural motifs.
steps: Observation (10 min): Look at real leaves, seed pods, feathers, kente/cloth samples — find the repeating units (motifs).
Analysis (10 min): How is a motif repeated? (Translation, reflection, rotation — shown with simple drawings).
Design (15 min): Each learner chooses 2 motifs from the nature table and drafts a border pattern in pencil.
Colour/texture (15 min): Complete the pattern with colour, focusing on neat repetition.
Gallery (5 min): Learners display work; 3 volunteers explain their motifs.
resources.assessment: Learner produces a repeating pattern with 2 motifs and consistent spacing.
resources.notes: Connect to kente, adinkra and batik — pattern mathematics lives in our own textile traditions.

resources.title: Safety in the Workshop and at Home
resources.subject: Career Technology
resources.contentStandard: Demonstrate knowledge and application of safety practices when using tools and materials.
resources.indicator: Identify hazards in workshops and kitchens and state safety rules that prevent them.
outcomes: Learner identifies at least 5 common hazards.
Learner matches each hazard to a safety rule.
steps: Starter (5 min): Show a picture of a messy workshop — 'What could go wrong here?' Collect hazards from the class.
Direct teaching (15 min): Hazard types — sharp tools, hot surfaces, electricity, spills, poor posture, loose clothing. Matching safety rules and personal protective equipment.
Hazard hunt (15 min): Groups inspect a mock setup (or classroom/kitchen area) and list hazards they find, then propose fixes.
Poster task (10 min): Each group makes one safety poster for a chosen area.
Recap (5 min): Class safety pledge.
resources.assessment: Learner identifies 5 hazards and states correct prevention for each.
resources.notes: Safety is a Career Technology exam favourite and a life skill — the two purposes reinforce each other.

resources.title: Greetings and Polite Expressions (Ghanaian Language)
resources.subject: Ghanaian Language
resources.contentStandard: Use appropriate greetings and courtesy expressions for different times and situations.
resources.indicator: Respond to and initiate greetings appropriately at different times of the day.
outcomes: Learner greets and responds appropriately for morning, afternoon and evening.
Learner uses 2 polite expressions (please, thank you) in role-play.
steps: Modeled dialogue (10 min): Teacher and helper perform time-of-day greetings in the local language; class echoes.
Chain drill (10 min): Round the class — each learner greets the next; variation: whisper greetings, sing greetings.
Market role-play (15 min): Buyers and sellers must greet, use 'please' and 'thank you' before any transaction happens.
Reflection (5 min): Why do greetings matter in our culture? (Respect, relationship, belonging).
resources.assessment: Learner initiates a correct greeting exchange for 2 different times of day.
resources.notes: Adapt all expressions to your local language — Twi, Ga, Ewe, Fante, Dagbani and others all differ. The structure stays the same.

resources.title: Needs vs. Wants — and Starting to Save (Susu Tracker)
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner distinguishes between needs and wants.
Learner sets one realistic savings goal and tracks it for 4 weeks.
resources.why: Children who learn early to separate what they must have from what they merely desire, and to set money aside little by little, grow into adults who can survive an emergency instead of borrowing at crisis prices. The susu habit — Ghana's own traditional saving system — makes saving normal, not strange.
steps: Sorting game (10 min): Learners sort picture/word cards (school bag, sweets, textbook, toy) into 'Need' vs 'Want' and defend the tricky ones.
Story/discussion (10 min): A short relatable scenario about a child saving pocket money for a goal — discuss what the child gave up and why it was worth it.
Activity (15 min): Learners design a simple 4-week susu savings tracker for a goal of their choice — each week they record the amount saved.
Class discussion: Why some purchases can wait — and what to do when pressure comes from friends.
resources.assessment: Learner sets one realistic savings goal and lists 2 needs vs. 2 wants correctly.
resources.notes: Ties to mathematics (money, counting) — run it alongside a Maths week on money for a double impact.

resources.title: Counting Ghanaian Money: Coins, Notes and Change
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner identifies all Ghanaian coins and common notes by their value.
Learner counts money up to GH¢50 and works out simple change.
resources.why: Every Ghanaian child handles money — at the market, for transport, for food. A child who can count money and check change confidently is protected from being cheated and is already doing mathematics without knowing it.
steps: Money hunt (5 min): Learners name coins and notes they have seen — 100 pesewas make GH¢1.
Identification (10 min): Real or picture money passed around — match each note/coin to its value; notice the security features and heroes on the notes.
Counting practice (10 min): Build given amounts with coins/notes (GH¢2.50, GH¢10, GH¢20) using paper money cut-outs.
Market role-play (10 min): Buyer and seller — buyer pays, seller checks, buyer counts the change out loud.
Wrap-up (5 min): One rule to remember: always count your change before walking away.
resources.assessment: Learner counts out 2 given amounts correctly and finds the right change for 3 of 4 purchases.
resources.notes: Involve a real trader story — how counting change fast is a market survival skill.

resources.title: Making a Simple Budget for My Money
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner explains what a budget is.
Learner creates a simple budget splitting money into saving, spending and sharing.
resources.why: A budget is not a punishment — it is a plan that makes your money go where YOU choose. Adults who budget survive lean months; adults who do not are always surprised. Teaching the 50-30-20 idea in a child-friendly form (spend-save-share) plants the habit early.
steps: Starter (5 min): 'You get GH¢20 for the week. By Wednesday it is gone. Where did it go?' Collect honest answers.
Direct teaching (10 min): A budget = a written plan before the money is spent. Introduce child-friendly splits: SPEND (daily needs), SAVE (a goal), SHARE (helping others/gifts).
Guided example (10 min): Budget GH¢10 of weekly money on the board — e.g., 5 spend / 3 save / 2 share; show how the save column grows over 4 weeks.
Individual budgets (15 min): Learners make their own budget for a stated weekly amount and goal, with amounts that must add up correctly.
Presentation (5 min): 3 learners present; class checks that the columns add up.
resources.assessment: Learner's budget columns add up to the total and include a saving line with a named goal.
resources.notes: Keep budgets real to their lives: transport, food, football cards, church/贡献 contributions.

resources.title: Mobile Money (MoMo) Safety
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner explains how MoMo works at a basic level (send, receive, withdraw).
Learner identifies at least 4 MoMo scam patterns and the correct response to each.
resources.why: Mobile money is Ghana's financial bloodstream — and scammers target it daily. Young people who cannot spot a fake MoMo prompt, a 'wrong transfer' trick, or a PIN-sharing con become victims within months of getting their first phone. This lesson is protection.
steps: Experience survey (5 min): Who has used or watched MoMo being used? What happens at the vendor kiosk?
How it works (10 min): Sending, receiving, withdrawing, the agent's role, and the PIN — your PIN is like the key to your room.

Scam gallery (15 min): Read out 4-5 real scam patterns — fake promotion texts ('You have won!'), wrong-transfer calls asking you to resend, agents asking for your PIN, 'help me cash out' requests from strangers, spoofed official numbers. For each: learners state the correct response.

Golden rules (10 min): Class co-creates the rules — never share your PIN (not even with family), never send money back to 'fix' a wrong transfer (verify first), check the name before confirming, report to the provider/police.
Role-play (5 min): One learner plays a scammer calling; the class refuses and reports correctly.
resources.assessment: Learner identifies the correct response in 4 of 5 scam scenarios.
resources.notes: Update the scam examples every term — scammers change tactics. Invite a vendor to speak if possible.

resources.title: Buy, Sell and Profit: Mini Market Day
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner explains cost, selling price and profit.
Learner runs a mini trading activity and calculates profit or loss.
resources.why: Entrepreneurship is not magic — it is arithmetic plus courage. Learners who buy, sell and count profit in a safe classroom market understand why traders greet you warmly, why prices move, and how their own small business could start one day.
steps: Concepts (10 min): Cost price, selling price, profit = selling price − cost, loss when the answer is negative. Work 3 examples on the board.
Group trading plan (15 min): Each group gets a mock GH¢50 — choose what to 'buy' (mock price list: toffees, exercise books, sachet water) and set selling prices with reasons.
Market day (20 min): Half the class sells, half buys with mock money; two rounds, then swap roles. Record every transaction on a sales sheet.
Profit audit (10 min): Each group computes total sales, total cost and profit/loss; discuss why some groups earned more (pricing, marketing, location).
Reflection (5 min): One lesson the group learned about trade.
resources.assessment: Learner's group calculates profit or loss correctly from their own recorded transactions.
resources.notes: Use mock money only — never real cash. This is a Maths+Business double lesson.

resources.title: Staying Safe Online
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner identifies safe online behaviour.
Learner recognises the risks of sharing personal information.
resources.why: The internet does not forget, and strangers online can appear kind while gathering information. A learner who understands what must never be shared — location, school, photos, phone numbers — and who can spot manipulation is far harder to harm.
steps: Discussion (10 min): What apps/sites do learners use, and what information do they ask for?
Direct teaching (15 min): Personal information that should never be shared publicly; recognising suspicious messages; the rule that people online may not be who they claim.
Scenario cards (15 min): Learners decide 'safe' or 'unsafe' for a series of short online situations and justify each call.
Wrap-up: Class rules for safe online behaviour, co-created with learners.
resources.assessment: Learner correctly identifies safe/unsafe behaviour in 4 out of 5 scenarios.
resources.notes: Pairs well with the JHS Computing curriculum — tag and schedule it next to a Computing lesson.

resources.title: Passwords and Personal Information
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner explains what makes a strong password.
Learner creates a strong, memorable password and states 3 rules for keeping it safe.
resources.why: A password is the lock on a child's first digital door. Weak passwords ('123456', birthdays, names) are broken in seconds. Learners who build strong passwords and refuse to share them — even with best friends — protect their accounts, their work and their identity.
steps: Demonstration (5 min): How quickly simple passwords are guessed — class guesses 'password', '123456', a birthday in seconds.
Strong password recipe (10 min): Long (at least 8), mixed (letters + numbers + symbols), not your name/birthday/phone, and a sentence trick: 'I love jollof 4 ever!' → Ilj4e!.
Create (15 min): Each learner drafts 2 strong passwords for an imaginary account and tests them against the class checklist.
Rules of keeping (5 min): Never write it where others can see, never tell anyone, change it if you suspect anything.
Quiz (5 min): Safe or risky? — sharing a password, using a birthday, writing it in a diary.
resources.assessment: Learner's 2 passwords pass all checklist criteria and learner states 3 keeping rules.
resources.notes: Practise the sentence-trick — it turns security into a game, not a lecture.

resources.title: Spotting Fake News and Misinformation
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner explains what misinformation is and why it spreads.
Learner applies 4 checks to decide whether a piece of information is trustworthy.
resources.why: False health claims, fake exam leaks and doctored photos spread faster than truth, and learners are prime targets because they forward first and think later. A learner with 4 quick verification checks becomes a household's immune system against nonsense.
steps: Hook (10 min): Show two similar-sounding claims — one true, one false — and vote: who already shared something that turned out false? (No shame — everyone has.)
Why it spreads (10 min): Emotional content, forwarded-many-times effect, money/scam motives, careless screenshots.

The 4 checks (15 min): 1) Who is the source and are they real? 2) Do trusted sources (GNA, major outlets, official pages) say the same? 3) Is the date current or recycled? 4) Does it beg you to share urgently?
Practice (10 min): 3 sample messages — class applies the 4 checks and gives a verdict with reasons.
Class rule (5 min): 'Check before you share' — co-signed poster.
resources.assessment: Learner applies the 4 checks and gives a correct verdict on 2 of 3 samples.
resources.notes: Never ridicule a learner for falling for a fake — praise the checking instead.

resources.title: Social Media Manners and Your Digital Footprint
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner explains what a digital footprint is.
Learner evaluates which posts help or harm a person's future.
resources.why: Everything posted today can be seen by a future employer, university or spouse. Learners who understand that the internet is a permanent public record post with care — and those who practice kindness online avoid becoming bullies or victims.
steps: Footprint demo (5 min): A chalk 'footprint trail' across the classroom floor — each step is a post that cannot be erased.
Case stories (10 min): Two short anonymised cases — a post that earned someone a scholarship opportunity, and one that cost someone a job. What made the difference?
The test (10 min): Before posting, ask — Would I be happy if my grandmother, my head teacher and a future employer all saw this? Learners classify 6 sample posts as post/never-post.
Kindness code (15 min): Draft a class social media code — no shaming, no fighting in comments, report bullies, ask before posting others' photos.
Commitment (5 min): Each learner writes one personal posting rule.
resources.assessment: Learner correctly classifies 5 of 6 sample posts and explains one consequence of a digital footprint.
resources.notes: Handle this with warmth, not fear — the goal is wise sharing, not silence.

resources.title: Using and Caring for a Computer or Phone
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner demonstrates careful handling of devices.
Learner names 5 device-care rules and 3 basic troubleshooting steps.
resources.why: Devices are expensive and many schools have few. A learner who handles equipment with care, keeps food and liquids away, and can try basic fixes (check power, restart, ask calmly) becomes the trusted class helper every school needs.
steps: Handling demo (10 min): Correct ways to carry, open, set down a laptop/phone; what hands must be (clean, dry) and what never comes near (food, water, dust, magnets).
Care rules (10 min): Class generates the rules list — clean hands, no pulling cables, no hugging the screen, keep off dusty surfaces, charge safely (not overnight on the bed).
Troubleshooting (10 min): The calm 3-step — check the power/battery, restart, report/ask. Practise the language: 'It is not working' is less useful than 'It will not turn on since this morning'.
Rotation practice (10 min): Stations where learners practise opening/closing/typing on a real device if available (or role-play with a cardboard laptop).
resources.assessment: Learner states 5 care rules and performs the calm 3-step troubleshooting aloud.
resources.notes: Pair learners with devices responsibly; rotate so everyone touches the machine.

resources.title: Handwashing and Germs
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner explains how germs spread and make us sick.
Learner demonstrates the correct handwashing steps at critical times.
resources.why: Diarrhoea and other preventable diseases spread mostly through dirty hands. Handwashing with soap at the right moments — after the toilet, before eating, after play — is the cheapest health technology in the world, and it starts with children who can do it properly.
steps: Glitter/germ demo (10 min): 'Glitter germs' on hands — shake a friend's hand, touch a book, watch germs travel. Then wash: water alone vs soap (why soap matters).
Correct technique (10 min): The steps — wet, soap, scrub palms, between fingers, backs, thumbs, nails, wrists, rinse, dry clean. Sing the 20-second song.
Critical times (10 min): When MUST we wash — after toilet, before eating/helping with food, after play, after touching animals, after coughing.
Practice (10 min): All learners wash at the Veronica bucket/station while a partner checks the steps.
Poster (5 min): Class handwashing promise poster.
resources.assessment: Learner demonstrates all handwashing steps and states 3 critical times.
resources.notes: Make the hygiene monitor a rotating honoured role — children enforce what they own.

resources.title: Personal Hygiene: Keeping Clean Every Day
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner lists the daily personal hygiene routine.
Learner explains why hygiene prevents disease and protects respect.
resources.why: At this age bodies change, sweat increases and peer opinion sharpens. A learner who bathes daily, brushes twice, wears clean clothes and keeps nails short avoids infections AND protects their confidence in public — hygiene is both health and dignity.
steps: Open discussion (10 min): What happens when someone is not clean? (Smell, skin rashes, ringworm, jiggers, teasing, illness.) Keep it factual, not mocking.
The daily routine (10 min): Bathing (soap all over, daily), brushing teeth twice a day, clean underpants/clothes, short clean nails, oiled hair, clean shoes.
Germ science link (5 min): Where dirt hides — nails, between toes, armpits, private parts (cleaned gently and privately).
Practical plan (15 min): Each learner writes a personal hygiene timetable (morning/evening) and a weekly laundry/nail day.
Hygiene kit talk (5 min): What every learner should own: soap, toothbrush, clean towel, slippers for the washroom.
resources.assessment: Learner's timetable covers bathing, brushing, nails, clothes and explains 2 diseases hygiene prevents.
resources.notes: Handle body changes respectfully and privately where needed — never single anyone out.

resources.title: Menstrual Hygiene: What Everyone Should Know
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learners (boys and girls) explain what menstruation is and that it is healthy and normal.
Girls demonstrate safe management of menstruation at school; boys demonstrate respectful support.
resources.why: Menstruation should cost a girl nothing — not a day of school, not her confidence. When boys are educated alongside girls, teasing ends and girls get support instead of shame. Missed school days from poor menstrual management are a major, quiet cause of falling grades.
steps: Framing (5 min): This is biology and health — every person in this room was born because of it. Ground rules: respect, no mocking, questions welcome.
The science (10 min): What menstruation is, the roughly monthly cycle, that it is a sign of healthy growth — using proper words (vagina, pad), not whispers.

Management (15 min): Practical — pads (disposable or reusable cloth), changing every 4-6 hours, washing, safe disposal (never in toilets that block), carrying supplies in a discreet bag, washing hands after.
Boys' role (5 min): No teasing ever; helping a friend who needs support; it is normal and respectful to know about it.
School plan (10 min): Map the school's support — where pads are kept, who to see (female teacher/counsellor), what to do if it starts during class. Class agrees the no-teasing rule.
resources.assessment: Learners state the 4 key management practices and the class adopts the no-teasing rule.
resources.notes: Girls who stay home during their period can miss up to 3 school days a month — this lesson is a girls'-education intervention. Provide a private follow-up channel.

resources.title: Caring for My Teeth
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner demonstrates correct brushing technique.
Learner names foods that harm teeth and 2 brushing rules.
resources.why: Toothache destroys concentration and sleep, and decaying teeth damage confidence with a smile. Children who learn brushing technique properly at this age keep the habit for life — and it costs almost nothing.
steps: Demo (10 min): Big toothbrush + big model mouth (or a clean comb as 'teeth') — brush in small circles, front, back, top, tongue; 2 minutes twice a day.
Foods talk (10 min): Sugary drinks/sweets feed the germs that make holes in teeth — anything very sweet or sticky needs care after.
Practise (10 min): All learners 'brush' the model mouth with correct circles; partners check technique.
Challenge (5 min): The 2-minute-twice-a-day chart — learners take home a tick-chart for one week.
resources.assessment: Learner demonstrates correct circular brushing and states 2 rules.
resources.notes: If some learners have no brush, arrange with a local chemist/PTA — never shame; teach everyone.

resources.title: Safe Food and Clean Water
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner states 4 rules of safe food handling.
Learner describes 2 ways to make water safer to drink.
resources.why: Typhoid and cholera travel through unsafe food and water, and school-age children are frequent victims. Learners who know to wash food, boil or treat water, cover it, and buy from clean vendors protect their whole household — many will manage family food one day.
steps: Germ journey (10 min): Trace how germs reach food — dirty hands, flies, dirty water, unwashed containers, dust.
Safe handling rules (15 min): Wash fruits/vegetables; cook thoroughly; keep food covered from flies; wash containers; hot food hot, cold food cold; when in doubt, throw it out.
Water treatment (10 min): Boiling (rolling boil for 1 minute), chlorine tablets/aquatabs per instructions, clean storage container with a lid and a treated cup or tap.
Spot-the-risk (5 min): Class critiques 4 pictures of food/water handling — safe or risky and why.
Home mission (5 min): Learners check one thing at home tonight (is drinking water covered?) and report tomorrow.
resources.assessment: Learner states 4 food rules and 2 water treatments correctly.
resources.notes: Respect local practice while teaching — build on what families already do right (covering pots, etc.).

resources.title: Malaria: Preventing the Sickness That Steals School Days
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner explains how malaria spreads and 3 ways to prevent it.
Learner identifies early signs of malaria and what to do.
resources.why: Malaria is a leading cause of missed school in Ghana. A child who sleeps under a treated net, helps drain stagnant water and tells an adult early about fever protects their own education — and this age group happily enforces net-sleeping at home.
steps: Story (10 min): The mosquito that bit Kofi at dusk by the water jar — trace the chain: stagnant water → mosquito → bite → fever.
Prevention (15 min): Sleep under an insecticide-treated net EVERY night and tuck it in; cover/empty standing water; wear covering clothes at dusk; window nets.
Signs and action (10 min): Fever, chills/shivering, headache, body weakness, vomiting — tell an adult IMMEDIATELY and go to the clinic; finish all medicine given.
Net campaign (5 min): Class 'Sleep in the Net' pledge — learners promise and encourage siblings.
materials: Picture cards of the malaria chain
resources.assessment: Learner states 3 prevention methods and the correct action for fever.
resources.notes: Myth-bust gently: malaria is not from unripe mango or heat — it needs the mosquito. Never self-treat with leftover drugs.

resources.title: Road Safety
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner states the safe road-crossing procedure.
Learner identifies safe places and behaviours near roads.
resources.why: Road traffic injuries are a top killer of Ghanaian school children, and most walk to school along busy roads. Children who stop-look-listen and understand that vehicles cannot always see them carry a skill that literally saves lives every day.
steps: Walk the route (10 min): Identify the roads learners cross; point out the dangers seen together (fast cars, no zebra, blind bends).
The crossing rule (10 min): STOP at the edge — LOOK right, left, right again — LISTEN for engines — WALK straight across, never run. Chant it; practise on a chalk-drawn road in the compound.

Safe behaviours (10 min): Use zebra crossings where they exist; cross at straight visible spots, never between parked cars or on bends; face oncoming traffic when walking on the roadside; hold a young child's hand.
Vehicle respect (5 min): A car cannot stop instantly — never run out for a ball; never wave at drivers to hurry.
Practice circuit (5 min): Groups rehearse stop-look-listen-walk on the chalk road.
resources.assessment: Learner performs the full crossing sequence correctly on the practice road.
resources.notes: Walk the actual school route with learners once a term — reality teaches faster than diagrams.

resources.title: Basic First Aid: Cuts, Burns and Fainting
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner demonstrates first aid for a small cut and a minor burn.
Learner states the correct response when someone faints.
resources.why: Injuries happen at home, on the farm, at football — and the first person on the scene is usually not a nurse. A learner who can clean a cut, cool a burn and lay a fainting person down safely can be the difference between a small scar and a serious infection.
steps: Golden rule (5 min): First aid helps; it does not replace the clinic. Always tell an adult / seek help for anything serious.

Cuts (10 min): Wash your hands first; clean the wound with clean water and soap around it; press with clean cloth to stop bleeding; cover with a clean dressing; do NOT apply pepper, mud or herbs to a wound.
Burns (10 min): Cool water on the burn for 10-20 minutes; do NOT burst blisters; do NOT apply toothpaste, oil or egg; cover loosely with clean cloth; get help for anything big.
Fainting (10 min): Lay the person flat, raise the legs slightly, loosen tight clothing, get fresh air, do NOT crowd or pour water on the face; when they wake, give small sips of water.
Practice pairs (10 min): One plays injured, one gives first aid, then swap; teacher corrects techniques.
resources.assessment: Learner demonstrates cut-care and burn-care steps in the right order.
resources.notes: Emphasise what NOT to do — pepper on wounds and toothpaste on burns are common harmful local habits. When unsure: call an adult or clinic.

resources.title: Emergency Numbers and What to Say
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner recalls key Ghana emergency numbers.
Learner delivers a clear emergency call with the 5 facts.
resources.why: In an emergency, minutes decide outcomes — and a caller who panics wastes them. A learner who knows the numbers and can state name, location and problem clearly turns fear into help.
steps: The numbers (10 min): 112 (national emergency), 191 (police), 192 (fire), 193 (ambulance) — plus family numbers every learner should know by heart (parent, neighbour, chief/assemblyman).
The 5 facts (10 min): WHO you are, WHERE you are (landmark, not just 'home'), WHAT happened, HOW many people need help, WHAT is being done. Write the sentence frame on the board.

Call practice (15 min): Pairs role-play — 'caller' and 'operator' — using scenario cards (fire at the market, motorcycle accident, collapsed classmate, suspicious stranger). Caller must deliver all 5 facts.
When NOT to call (5 min): Prank calls waste lives and are punishable — discuss why.
Memorise (5 min): All learners recite the numbers.
resources.assessment: Learner recites the 4 numbers and delivers all 5 facts in a role-play call.
resources.notes: Send the number poster home — the whole family should have it near the door.

resources.title: My Body Belongs to Me: Saying No and Telling a Trusted Adult
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner states that their body belongs to them.
Learner demonstrates the safety steps: say no, get away, tell a trusted adult — and keeps telling until believed.
resources.why: Children are safest when they know, in simple and certain words, that their body is theirs, that no one may touch them in ways that feel wrong or secret, and that telling a trusted adult is always right — never something to fear. Clear, age-appropriate protection education prevents abuse and gives children the words to report it.
steps: Ownership (5 min): 'Your body is YOURS. Nobody may touch it in a way that makes you uncomfortable — not a stranger, not a relative, not a friend — nobody.' (Use proper words for private parts: the parts covered by underwear.)
The 3 steps (10 min): SAY NO loudly — GET AWAY to people — TELL a trusted adult (parent, teacher, auntie). And if the first adult does not act, TELL ANOTHER — keep telling until someone helps.

Tricky situations (10 min): Short scenarios — a gift with a 'secret' attached, anyone who asks to keep a 'secret' about touching, anyone who asks a child to go somewhere alone. Secret gifts and touching secrets are ALWAYS reported.
Practice voices (10 min): Every learner practises saying 'NO!' loudly and role-plays telling a trusted adult — make the words easy to say out loud.
Warm close (5 min): Naming their trusted adults (each learner names 3) and the teacher's own door is always open.
materials: Class poster: My Body Belongs to Me
resources.assessment: Learner demonstrates the say-no-get-away-tell sequence and names 3 trusted adults.
resources.notes: Delivered calmly and matter-of-factly, this lesson is protective, not frightening. Follow your school's safeguarding protocol for any disclosures — listen, never promise secrecy, report to the designated person.

resources.title: Speaking and Listening: Clear Communication
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner demonstrates active listening behaviours.
Learner gives a clear 1-minute talk with a beginning, middle and end.
resources.why: Almost every job, friendship and exam interview runs on communication. Learners who can look at a listener, organise three points and speak audibly — and who listen without interrupting — are immediately distinguishable in interviews and in class.
steps: Listening first (10 min): The listening rules — eyes on speaker, mouth closed, thinking about the words, wait then ask. Demonstrate a bad listener (comic), then a good one.
Telephone game (10 min): Message relay round the class — shows how meaning corrupts without care; discuss why repetition and clarity matter.
Structure recipe (10 min): My name and topic — 3 points (First…, Second…, Finally…) — my conclusion. Learners draft a 1-minute talk on 'My best day in school' using the frame.
Speaking circles (15 min): Groups of 4 — each speaks 1 minute while 3 listeners score eye-contact, voice and structure; rotate twice.
Class showcase (5 min): 2 volunteers present to the whole class.
resources.assessment: Learner delivers a 1-minute talk using the 3-part frame while listeners report active listening.
resources.notes: Shy learners start with 30 seconds and a seated position — growth, not perfection, is the goal.

resources.title: Teamwork: Working Together in Groups
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner states 3 rules of good teamwork.
Learner completes a group task where every member contributes.
resources.why: From farming to football to offices, Ghanaians achieve in groups. Children who learn early to share tasks, wait their turn, include the quiet one and finish the job together carry the skill every employer and community depends on.
steps: Tower challenge (15 min): Groups build the tallest paper tower — observe and afterwards ask: who shared materials? who listened to whose idea? did anyone get left out?
The 3 rules (10 min): 1) Everyone's idea is heard. 2) Tasks are shared — everyone has a job. 3) We finish together and help anyone who is stuck.
Roles (10 min): Introduce roles — leader, materials keeper, timekeeper, presenter — and re-run a mini task with roles assigned.
Reflection (5 min): What made the best team the best?
materials: Paper, bottle tops or blocks for towers
resources.assessment: Learner states the 3 rules and their group role; every member contributes visibly.
resources.notes: Rotate roles every group task so the quiet learners get leadership turns.

resources.title: Solving Disagreements Without Fighting
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner uses the 4-step peaceful problem-solving sequence.
Learner identifies anger warning signs and one calm-down strategy.
resources.why: Fights destroy friendships, cause suspensions and escalate into injuries — yet almost every school fight starts as a small disagreement handled badly. Learners who own a peaceful sequence (and know how to cool anger first) become peacemakers instead of combatants.
steps: Anatomy of a fight (10 min): Replay a familiar small conflict — what escalated it? (insults, audiences, pride, refusing to listen).

Calm down first (5 min): Anger signs (hot face, tight fists, loud voice) and calm-down tools — breathe slowly 5 times, walk away, count to 20, splash water. 'Never solve anything while your body is boiling.'

The 4 steps (10 min): 1) Each side states what happened WITHOUT insults (I-statements: 'I feel angry when…'). 2) Each listens and repeats the other's view. 3) Both suggest fair solutions. 4) Agree on one and shake.
Role-plays (15 min): Scenario pairs (football foul, borrowed book damaged, seat disputes) run the 4 steps; class watches for insults and fair solutions.
Peace pact (5 min): Class code — insults stop disagreements; fists end friendships.
resources.assessment: Learner runs the 4 steps in a role-play without insults and agrees a fair solution.
resources.notes: Teach bystanders too: the audience decides whether a fight happens. Laughing fuels it; 'cool it' starves it.

resources.title: Managing My Time
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner explains the difference between urgent and important tasks.
Learner builds a personal after-school timetable.
resources.why: Learners who reach JHS without time habits drown in homework, chores and football. A child who plans the evening — homework first, chores, play, sleep at a set hour — walks into JHS with an advantage that lasts through BECE year.
steps: Time audit (10 min): Learners estimate yesterday's hours — school, chores, homework, play, screens, sleep. Where did it go?

Urgent vs important (10 min): Sort task cards — urgent AND important (homework due tomorrow) vs urgent only (TV now) vs important not urgent (reading daily). Homework and revision live in the important zone.
Building the timetable (15 min): Fixed items first (school, chores, dinner), then homework block, then play — each learner drafts a realistic personal evening timetable with times.
Reality check (5 min): Swap timetables with a friend — is anything impossible? Fix it.
Trial week (5 min): Run it for one week and mark each day kept/missed.
resources.assessment: Learner's timetable places homework before play, with realistic times, and the learner explains the urgent/important difference.
resources.notes: Chores are real in Ghanaian homes — plan WITH them, not against them, or the timetable dies in week one.

resources.title: Setting Goals and Building a Study Plan
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner writes a SMART goal.
Learner converts a goal into a weekly study plan with specific subjects and times.
resources.why: JHS learners carry the BECE dream — but dreams without plans stay dreams. A learner who writes 'I want aggregate 6' and then books Mathematics for Monday evenings and English for Wednesday evenings has converted hope into a schedule, which is the only thing that actually produces results.
steps: Dream to goal (10 min): Each learner names their dream (school, trade, profession) and the grades it needs. Then sharpen it SMART — Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound. Example: 'Score at least 70% in Mathematics by end of Term 1'.
Gap analysis (10 min): Where am I now in each subject? What is the gap? Which subjects need the most hours? (Honesty required — the plan is for them, not the teacher.)

The weekly plan (20 min): Fixed anchors first (school, chores, church/mosque), then subject blocks — weakest subject gets the best hours; every evening has ONE named subject; short breaks every 30-40 minutes; weekends for revision + rest.
Commitment (5 min): Sign the plan; choose an accountability partner who checks it weekly.
Review loop (5 min): Every Sunday — what worked, what did not, adjust next week.
resources.assessment: Learner's plan names subjects and times for the week and contains a correctly written SMART goal.
resources.notes: Print the plan and give it to the parent/guardian — home support doubles follow-through.

resources.title: Exam Preparation and Calm Under Pressure
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner builds an exam-preparation countdown plan.
Learner uses 2 in-exam strategies: time budgeting and question triage.
resources.why: BECE decides school placements, and panic wastes marks as reliably as ignorance does. Learners who rehearse the exam-day routine — sleep, time-per-question, easy questions first, never leaving blanks — convert their real knowledge into real marks.
steps: Countdown plan (15 min): Working backwards from exam day — last month (cover weak topics), last week (revise notes and past questions, no new topics), last 3 days (light review, early sleep), exam eve (pack pens/pencils/rules, sleep early).

The exam-hall routine (15 min): Read instructions twice; budget minutes per question from total marks; answer EASY questions first to bank marks; mark hard ones and return; NEVER leave a blank — an attempted answer can score; keep 10 minutes to check.
Calm body (10 min): The physical tools — breathe in 4, hold 4, out 4 twice; feet flat, shoulders down; skip nothing from breakfast; no all-night cramming (sleep converts practice into recall).
Mock mini-exam (5 min): 5 questions in 4 minutes using the routine — feel the difference the strategy makes.
Debrief (5 min): What will you change about your last exam approach?
resources.assessment: Learner completes the mock mini-exam using time budgeting and scores a stated personal improvement target.
resources.notes: Normalize nerves: a racing heart means the body is ready — the routine channels it.

resources.title: Building Confidence and Self-Esteem
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner identifies 2 personal strengths with evidence.
Learner replaces one negative self-statement with a growth statement.
resources.why: At JHS age, self-talk becomes destiny — the learner who says 'I am just not a Maths person' stops trying, and the belief itself causes the failure. Learners who can name their strengths and re-frame weakness as 'not yet' attempt more, persist longer, and stand taller.
steps: Quiet poll (5 min): Anonymous cards — 'Write one thing you wish you were better at.' Read a few aloud; the room realises everyone carries doubts.
Strengths hunt (10 min): Each learner lists 3 strengths WITH evidence ('I am patient — I taught my younger brother to ride a bike'). Friends add one strength they see in each other.
The 'yet' skill (10 min): Reframe drill — 'I cannot do fractions' → 'I cannot do fractions YET — I will practise 15 minutes daily.' Contrast fixed vs growth statements on the board.
Confident body (10 min): Stand tall, chin up, speak at the back of the room — practise introducing yourself with the strong posture; note how it changes the feeling.
Affirmation chain (10 min): Each learner receives 2 one-line strengths from classmates to keep in their notebook.
resources.assessment: Learner states 2 strengths with real evidence and one 'yet' reframe.
resources.notes: Protect the vulnerable during the strengths exchange — model one round yourself first.

resources.title: Resisting Negative Peer Pressure
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner identifies pressure situations common at their age.
Learner demonstrates 3 refusal techniques with confident body language.
resources.why: Truancy, smoking, alcohol, gambling and early relationships rarely start with a stranger — they start with a friend saying 'just try it'. Learners who own rehearsed refusal lines and a ready exit plan keep their goals while keeping their friends where possible.
steps: Pressure map (10 min): Anonymous box — 'The hardest thing friends push you to do.' List the real pressures on the board (anonymously).
Understanding the pull (10 min): Why it is hard — fear of losing friends, wanting to belong, curiosity. Be honest: good people get pulled too.

The refusal toolkit (15 min): 1) Simple no with a reason — 'No, I have training tomorrow.' 2) Broken record — repeat your no calmly. 3) Flip the plan — 'Let's go and play football instead.' Add confident body: stand straight, eye contact, plain voice.
Pressure role-plays (10 min): Pairs act the pressure and the refusal using all 3 techniques; class scores believability.
Ally list (5 min): Each learner names 2 people they can call or sit with when pressure gets heavy.
resources.assessment: Learner demonstrates all 3 refusal techniques in role-play with confident delivery.
resources.notes: Distinguish refusing the act from rejecting the friend — 'I am not doing it' can be followed by 'but I will see you at break'.

resources.title: Honesty, Integrity and Responsibility
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner explains honesty and integrity in child language.
Learner accepts responsibility for own actions in a scenario.
resources.why: Trust is the currency of every classroom, home and nation. A child who owns mistakes ('I forgot it — it was me') instead of blaming others grows into the adult who keeps promises, handles money honestly and is trusted with responsibility.
steps: Story (10 min): The child who returned the lost money — what did people say about that child afterwards?
Concepts in child words (10 min): Honest = you tell the truth even when it is hard. Responsible = you own what you did and fix what you broke.
Puppet scenarios (15 min): Puppets face choices — broke a plate, forgot homework, found a pencil — class advises each puppet and praises the responsible choice.
Class responsibility jobs (5 min): Every learner gets a small classroom duty (water keeper, chalk monitor, board cleaner) — responsibility is practised, not preached.
resources.assessment: Learner responds honestly in a puppet scenario and performs their class duty for one week.
resources.notes: When a child confesses honestly, thank the courage BEFORE addressing the fault — it keeps truth-telling alive.

resources.title: My Rights and Responsibilities as a Child
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner lists 4 rights of the child (Ghana's Children's Act 1992, Act 560).
Learner matches each right to a matching responsibility.
resources.why: Ghana's Children's Act (1992, Act 560) protects every child's right to life, education, health, shelter and protection from harm — but rights land best when learners see the mirror: my right to education carries my responsibility to attend and learn. Knowing both protects children from abuse AND from entitlement.
steps: Starter (10 min): 'Do children have rights? Who decides?' Introduce the Children's Act 1992 (Act 560) and the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child (Ghana has ratified).

Rights gallery (15 min): Posters around the room — right to education, health care, shelter, protection from harm and forced labour, play/rest, name and nationality. Groups visit each and note examples.

The mirror (10 min): Every right has a partner responsibility — right to education ↔ go to school and learn; right to food/shelter ↔ respect and help at home; right to protection ↔ obey safety rules and report harm.
Real-life check (10 min): Scenarios — a child kept out of school to trade all day; a child beaten brutally — which rights? What should happen? (Report: teacher, Social Welfare, police).
Charter (5 min): Class rights-and-responsibilities charter signed by all.
resources.assessment: Learner lists 4 rights and pairs each with its matching responsibility.
resources.notes: Report harm through teachers or the Department of Social Welfare — give learners the real channel, not vague advice.

resources.title: Community Service: Lending a Hand
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner explains what community service is and why it matters.
The class plans and completes one small community service project.
resources.why: Citizenship is a muscle — it grows only by use. A class that sweeps the clinic waiting area, reads to the KG class, or clears a choked gutter learns that 'community' is not a social studies word but a place they can change with their own hands.
steps: What and why (10 min): Community service = giving time/skill without payment. Examples: hospital/clinic help, cleaning markets and gutters, helping the aged, tree planting, neighbourhood watch support.
Needs hunt (10 min): 'What problem near our school could we fix in 2 hours with no money?' List ideas and vote.
Planning (15 min): Choose one — assign jobs, materials, date, safety rules, and what permission/adult supervision is needed.
Do it (next week — 90-120 min): Execute the project with photos for the class report.
Reflect (10 min): What changed? What did WE learn? Who noticed? (This builds the service habit, not a one-off event.)
materials: Depends on project — brooms, gloves, rubbish bags, watering cans
resources.assessment: Class completes the project and each learner states one way the community benefited.
resources.notes: Keep projects small, safe and repeatable. Invite the assembly member/chief to see the work — community recognition compounds.

resources.title: Keeping My Community Clean: Waste Management
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner explains how poor waste disposal causes disease and flooding.
Learner practices the waste hierarchy: reduce, reuse, recycle, proper disposal.
resources.why: Choked gutters flood Accra every rainy season and mosquitoes breed in every discarded sachet. Learners who sort waste, refuse single-use where possible, and keep their compound clean are acting on the environmental lesson Ghana most needs.
steps: The chain (10 min): Trace it — thrown sachet → choked gutter → flood → malaria/cholera → missed school. Learners draw the chain.

Sort it (15 min): Waste sorting game — organic (food peels → compost pit), plastics (reuse/recycle), papers (burn ONLY where approved — prefer reuse), hazardous (batteries, broken glass — special handling).
The hierarchy (10 min): Reduce (use less packaging), Reuse (bottles as pen holders, sachets as seedling bags), Recycle (where collection exists), Dispose properly (covered bins, not gutters/bushes).
School audit (5 min): Walk the compound — where does our waste actually go? One fix we propose this week.
Action (5 min): Class adopts the compound cleaning rota.
resources.assessment: Learner sorts 8 of 10 waste items correctly and states 2 diseases poor waste causes.
resources.notes: Composting peels into the school garden turns this lesson into free fertiliser — circular, visible, memorable.

resources.title: Tolerance: Respecting Our Differences
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner explains tolerance and its limits (respect does not require agreement).
Learner demonstrates respectful disagreement on a real difference.
resources.why: Ghana's classrooms mix tribes, faiths, languages and abilities — and insults about tribe, religion or disability are often a learner's first experience of exclusion. Learners who can disagree without dehumanising keep the peace at home and defend it as adults.
steps: Our mix (10 min): Anonymous mapping — languages spoken at home, faiths, home regions. The class IS the diversity lesson.
Respect vs agreement (10 min): Tolerance means living respectfully WITH difference, not pretending it does not exist. Name the boundary: beliefs may differ; mocking does neither side honour.
Tribal/religious jokes audit (10 min): Learners recall common jokes/stereotypes and examine the harm — 'funny to some, degrading to the target, dangerous in a crowd'.

Practice dialogue (10 min): Pairs with different views on a mild topic (best football team, best food) must state their view AND summarise the other's fairly — the discipline of disagreement without insult.
Class covenant (5 min): One line everyone signs: 'Here, no tribe, faith or language is a joke.'
resources.assessment: Learner participates in a respectful disagreement and states the class covenant's purpose.
resources.notes: Teacher sets the tone: correct bias instantly, quietly and consistently — tolerance is caught from adults first.

resources.title: Filling Forms and Writing a Simple Letter
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner fills a simple form completely and correctly.
Learner writes a short personal note/letter with the essential parts.
resources.why: Adult life is paperwork — school admission forms, MoMo registration, clinic cards, job applications. A learner who can read instructions, fill every field neatly and write a clear note will never need someone else to manage their own basic documents.
steps: Form anatomy (10 min): A real form projected/drawn — label fields (name, date of birth, address, signature), spot instructions ('Use BLOCK LETTERS', 'Tick one'), and the traps (empty fields, wrong date format).
Guided fill (10 min): Class fills a mock school club form together, field by field, checking each against instructions.
Neatness discipline (5 min): Write withIN lines, no crossings-out, ask before guessing, always sign where signed-off is required.
Simple letter (10 min): The 5 essential parts — date, greeting, body (why I am writing), closing, name. Write a note requesting permission for a school trip.
Check swap (10 min): Partners audit each other's form and letter against the checklist.
resources.assessment: Learner's form has zero empty required fields and the letter contains all 5 parts.
resources.notes: Bring REAL forms where possible (a blank clinic card) — authenticity makes the skill obvious.

resources.title: Basic Cooking and Kitchen Safety
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner follows a recipe with correct sequencing.
Learner applies 5 kitchen safety rules.
resources.why: Feeding yourself safely is independence. Learners who can prepare a simple, balanced dish — and know to turn pot handles inward, cut away from fingers, and never pour water onto hot oil — protect themselves daily and impress their households within a week.
steps: Menu and maths (10 min): Choose one simple dish (e.g., plain rice and stew or groundnut soup starter) — read the recipe, list ingredients and cost them from a mock market list.
Mise en place (10 min): Wash hands, tie hair, clean the station, gather and wash all ingredients and utensils BEFORE any heat — professional habit from day one.
Safety briefing (5 min): Pot handles turned inward, knife cuts away from fingers, dry hands for electricity, fire discipline, never leave cooking unattended.
Cook (25 min): Execute step by step with roles (washing, cutting under supervision, stirring, timing).
Taste, review, wash up (10 min): Eat together, then clean the kitchen completely — cooking is not finished until the kitchen is clean.
resources.assessment: The dish is completed per recipe sequence and learners state all 5 safety rules.
resources.notes: Allergy and religion check BEFORE choosing the dish. Mix cooking with nutrition talk — protein, vegetables, less oil.

resources.title: Simple Repairs: Sewing a Button and Mending a Tear
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner sews a button securely.
Learner makes a simple straight mend on a small tear.
resources.why: A torn uniform or lost button sends children to the tailor for money many families do not have — or to school looking unkempt. A learner with a needle, thread and 10 minutes of skill fixes both, and the confidence of mending one's own things lasts forever.
steps: Tools and threading (10 min): Needle, thread, scissors — thread the needle (double for strength), knot the end. Patience drill — everyone threads successfully before moving on.
Button sewing (15 min): Position, anchor stitch, pass through the button holes 4-6 times, anchor underneath, knot and cut. Partners inspect firmness.
Simple mend (15 min): Straight tear — bring edges together, anchor, straight/ladder stitch, knot on the wrong side.
Care kit (5 min): The pocket repair kit — needle, thread, spare button — every learner should know where theirs is.
resources.assessment: Learner's button survives a firm tug and the mend holds.
resources.notes: Safety with needles is non-negotiable — count needles out and in. This is a calm, meditative lesson many learners love.

resources.title: Planting and Caring for a School Garden
resources.subject: Life Skills
outcomes: Learner plants a seed correctly with right depth and spacing.
The class maintains a garden bed through germination to transplanting/harvest.
resources.why: A garden teaches patience, responsibility and where food actually comes from — and it feeds the school kitchen. Children who water a bed daily and watch week by week learn agriculture, science and discipline in one living classroom.
steps: Site and soil (10 min): Choose the spot — sun, water access, fenced from animals. Test soil feel (sand/silt/clay) and plan the beds.
Planting (15 min): Choose fast, forgiving crops — okro, pepper, garden eggs, tomato, kontomire. Correct depth (2x seed size), spacing, watering-in gently. Label each bed with crop and date.
Care rota (10 min): Assign watering days/teams, weeding duty, pest watch (check leaves weekly), and a garden diary — one learner records observations each day.
Watch and learn (10 min): Set the observation routine — measure growth weekly, count leaves, note weather. Connect to Science lessons on plants.
Harvest plan (5 min): Decide together who benefits — school kitchen, tasting day, or sale into the susu fund (life-skills loop!).
resources.assessment: Learner plants at correct depth/spacing and performs their care-duty reliably over 2 weeks.
resources.notes: Start tiny — one bed beats a failed farm. Container/sack gardens work where land is scarce.

resources.title: Storytelling Club (Lower Primary)
resources.subject: Extracurricular
outcomes: Builds oral language, listening and confidence with zero equipment.
steps: Teacher or a learner tells a short story with actions.
Learners retell the story in pairs, adding one new detail.
Weekly rotation: 'storyteller of the week' tells a family or community story.
End of term: class story festival with simple costumes from home.
resources.assessment: Participation and retelling confidence observed over the term.
resources.notes: Zero-budget activity. Links to Ghanaian Language and English oral skills.

resources.title: Junior Debate Club (Upper Primary)
resources.subject: Extracurricular
